About: the conical pendulum — launch speed, string angle, and angular momentum

Source

Concept
A bob (m = 0.5 kg) on a light string (L = 1 m) launched horizontally from a held angle: what does the string's angle do at different launch speeds, and what happens to the bob's angular momentum about the suspension?
Serves
Investigating whether a conical pendulum can circle steadily at any launch speed, and how the components of its angular momentum about the suspension behave through the motion.
Inquiry
Six sealed prediction cards: rest, gentle, hard, which component survives, the skater consequence, and what the launch sets.
Misconception
"Conserved means it always has the same universal value." The cards probe what a conserved quantity's value actually depends on.

Pedagogy principles applied

Predict before revealEvery card commits a choice before the bob is launched; the scene then confirms or refutes it.
Invariant made visibleThe angular-momentum vector sweeps at the suspension while its vertical mark on the axis stands perfectly still.
Earned landmarkThe critical-speed tick on the slider stays hidden until the hunt cards are answered.
Honest integrationThe 3D motion is the sim's own RK4 spherical pendulum; L_z is read from the state, not echoed from a formula.
Target the misconceptionCard 6 makes the half-speed launch give exactly half L_z — conservation fixes whatever the launch created.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Launch at rest

Set the initial angle to 30° and the launch speed to zero. Before releasing the bob, predict the path it follows.

2 · Gentle launch

Keep the angle at 30° and set the launch speed to 1 m s⁻¹. Before launching, predict what the angle of the string does.

3 · Hard launch

Keep the angle at 30° and set the launch speed to 2.5 m s⁻¹. Before launching, predict what the angle does now.

4 · Which part survives

The tension acts along the string and gravity acts straight down. Before running any of the cases again, predict which part of the bob's angular momentum about the suspension point these two forces can never change.

5 · Rate of circling

Return to the 30°, 1 m s⁻¹ launch, in which the string swings inward. Before launching, predict how fast the bob circles the vertical axis as the string comes in.

6 · Half the speed

For the steady launch at 30° the readout shows L_z = 0.42 kg m² s⁻¹. Before launching again at the same angle but at half that speed, predict the value of L_z and what it does afterwards.

The Physics

The conical pendulum · what it is about, the physics behind it, and what every control does

A bob on a 1 m string, held out at an angle and launched sideways. Two sliders set the whole experiment; everything else on screen is there to tell you what happened.

1What you'll work out

  • Why a conical pendulum holds its angle at one launch speed — and what it does at every other speed.
  • Which part of the bob's angular momentum about the suspension point survives the motion, and which parts don't.
  • What the launch itself fixes for good, and what that forces the bob to do as the string swings.

JEE / NCERT Class 11 — circular motion, the conical pendulum, and angular momentum about a point.

2What this simulation shows

The bob hangs from a fixed point on a light string of length L = 1 m and has mass m = 0.5 kg. You hold it out at an angle θ₀, then release it with a level, sideways speed v₀. From that instant nothing touches it but the string and gravity — the sim integrates the real spherical pendulum, so the path you see is the motion, not an animation of a formula.

The one thing to watch is the string angle. It can hold steady, swing inwards, or swing outwards, and which of those happens is decided entirely by the two numbers you set before releasing.

01

Why does the string angle move at all?

The steady circle at the sim's default 30°, computed from m = 0.5 kg, L = 1 m, g = 9.8 m s⁻². Two force equations, one closed triangle.
  • A circle at a fixed angle needs the string to do two jobs at once: hold the bob up (FT cos θ = mg) and pull it round (FT sin θ = mv²/r).
  • Divide one by the other and the tension cancels: v² = gL sin θ tan θ. At a given angle that is one speed, not a range — 1.6820 m s⁻¹ at 30°.
  • Launch slower and the inward pull is more than the circle needs, so the bob falls inward. Launch faster and it swings out. The angle only sits still at exactly vc.
The two components, and the single speed that satisfies both.
02

Which part of the angular momentum survives?

Tension acts along the string, so its torque about O is exactly zero. Gravity's torque about O is horizontal — and a horizontal torque cannot change a vertical component.
  • The bob's full angular-momentum vector sweeps a cone as the bob goes round: its length changes, its direction changes.
  • Only Lz, the vertical component, is conserved — the mark on the axis in the sim stands perfectly still while the vector above it swings.
  • This is why "angular momentum is conserved" needs an about-what and a which-component. Neither the magnitude nor Lx, Ly is conserved here.
The steady 30° launch: the vector's length is 0.8410, of which 0.4205 is vertical. The horizontal part is the piece that swings.
Three quantities, one conserved. The readout tracks the one that is.
03

What does the launch actually set?

The launch is horizontal, so the whole speed goes into circulation: Lz is fixed the instant you let go.
  • A conserved quantity does not have one universal value. Its value is whatever your launch created — and then it is stuck with it.
  • Halve the launch speed at the same angle and Lz is exactly halved, then held at that new value for ever after.
04

In or out? One curve tells you before you launch.

With Lz fixed, θ moves in a one-dimensional landscape. The centrifugal barrier is what stops the string ever reaching the axis.
The same launch angle on three different curves — because each launch speed fixes a different Lz. Turning points computed from the sim's own θ-equation.
  • A horizontal launch means θ̇ = 0, so the energy line always starts on the curve at 30°. Where the curve's minimum sits relative to 30° is the whole answer.
  • v₀ = 1 m s⁻¹: the minimum is at 23.04°, left of the launch — θ runs in, to a turning point at 17.73°, and oscillates between the two.
  • v₀ = 2.5 m s⁻¹: the minimum has moved out to 36.72° — θ runs out, to 45.08°.
  • v₀ = vc: the launch is the minimum. Nothing to roll down; the angle holds.
05

Why does it circle faster as the string comes in?

The same statement as the skater pulling her arms in — here the string does the pulling.
  • Lz is fixed, and Lz = mL²sin²θ·φ̇. If sin θ shrinks, φ̇ must grow to compensate — and it grows as the square.
  • The gentle launch goes from 30° to 17.73°: sin θ falls by a factor 1.641, so φ̇ rises by 1.641² = 2.6945, from 2.0000 to 5.3890 rad s⁻¹.
  • It is not that the bob speeds up because it fell. It is that the one quantity nothing can change forces the rate up as the circle shrinks.
Circulation rate against string angle at the gentle launch's fixed Lz = 0.2500.
For the steady circle only: the lap time and the tension, both from the angle alone.
06

The traps they'll set for you

  • "Conserved means it always has the same value." It means it never changes after you set it. Launch at half the speed and Lz is half — and that half is then conserved just as firmly.
  • "Angular momentum is conserved here." Only its vertical component, and only about the suspension point. The magnitude |L| visibly changes as the bob rises and falls.
  • "A faster launch needs a smaller angle, because the bob is harder to hold up." The opposite: faster than vc and the string swings out. Steeper angles need more speed, not less.
  • "It circles faster because it has fallen and gained speed." Energy does rise as θ falls, but the rate of circling is fixed by Lz/sin²θ alone — quadrupling if sin θ halves, whatever the energy is doing.
  • "Launch it horizontally and it must go round in a circle." Only at exactly vc. Every other horizontal launch gives a wobble between two angles.
07

Ninety-second self-test

Launch from a 30° hold with v₀ = 0. What is Lz, and what does the bob do?

Lz = mv₀L sin θ₀ = 0. With no vertical angular momentum there is no centrifugal barrier at all, so θ is free to reach zero: the bob swings in the vertical plane straight through the lowest point, like an ordinary pendulum.

Does the tension do any work on the bob?

No — the string is inextensible, so the bob's velocity is always perpendicular to it. That is also why the tension contributes no torque about O: it acts along the position vector from O. Gravity is the only thing doing work, and the only thing exerting a torque.

At 30° the steady launch is 1.6820 m s⁻¹. Launch at 1 m s⁻¹ instead and the string swings in to 17.73°. Why doesn't it keep going to the axis?

Because Lz ≠ 0 and the centrifugal term Lz²/(2mL²sin²θ) blows up as sin θ → 0. The θ-motion hits a wall it cannot climb, turns round, and heads back out — the string can never reach the vertical unless Lz is exactly zero.

Two launches at the same angle, speeds v and 2v. Compare their Lz and their circulation rates at the moment of launch.

Lz doubles (it is linear in v₀), and since φ̇ = Lz/(mL²sin²θ) at the same θ, the launch circulation rate doubles too. What differs afterwards is where each one goes: the slower one may swing in, the faster one out, depending on where each sits relative to its own vc.
